title: Tagliatelle ai funghi
subtitle: Tagliatelle with wild mushrooms
excerpt: Egg tagliatelle tossed with a buttery sauce of mixed wild mushrooms, garlic, parsley, and a splash of white wine. A simple pasta that depends entirely on the quality of the mushrooms.
sourceNotes: Classic Italian pasta preparation, typical of northern Italy in autumn when porcini and chanterelles are available. Variations appear throughout the cooking literature of Emilia-Romagna and Piedmont.

content.text: Tagliatelle ai funghi needs very good mushrooms. Use a mixture: dried porcini rehydrated and combined with fresh chestnut or shiitake, or a bag of prepared wild mushrooms from a market stall. The sauce is brief and clean: butter, garlic, wine, parsley, pasta water to bind.

items.prepNote: or a mix of wild mushrooms, sliced
soaked in 150 ml hot water for 20 minutes, liquid reserved

content.text: Soak the dried porcini in 150 ml hot water for 20 minutes. Drain, reserving the soaking liquid. Rinse the porcini to remove any grit and chop roughly.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil for the pasta.

Heat the olive oil and 25 g butter in a wide frying pan over high heat. Add the fresh mushrooms in a single layer. Do not stir for 2 minutes; let them brown. Toss and continue cooking for 3 more minutes. Add the porcini and cook for 1 minute more.

Reduce heat to medium. Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute. Pour in the wine and let it bubble until reduced by half. Pour in the reserved porcini soaking liquid, keeping back the last tablespoon which may be gritty.
Cook the {{pasta-dried}} in the boiling water until 1 minute short of the packet time. Reserve a ladleful of pasta water, then drain.

Add the pasta to the mushroom pan. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute, adding pasta water to loosen into a saucy consistency. Remove from heat, add the remaining 25 g butter and the parsley, toss to combine. Season and serve immediately with Parmesan if using.

items.symptom: The mushrooms are watery and pale
items.cause: Pan overcrowded or heat too low
items.fix: Fry mushrooms in two batches in a very hot pan. They should colour before they release moisture.

items.cause: Not enough sauce or pasta left to drain too long
items.fix: Add more pasta water. Dress the pasta immediately after draining.

items.cause: Insufficient salt or porcini soaking liquid discarded
items.fix: Season generously. The porcini liquid adds depth; use all of it except the last gritty tablespoon.
Toss over higher heat for 30 seconds to reduce. The starch in the pasta water will help it bind.

content.text: Autumn is mushroom season in northern Italy, and pasta ai funghi appears on restaurant menus from October through December alongside game and polenta. Porcini are the prestige ingredient; chanterelles are more delicate and fragrant; chestnut mushrooms give body at lower cost. The dish works with any single mushroom or combination. Dried porcini are the base note that ties the sauce together whatever else goes in.
